Learning notes: Markets Overview

Browse 170 simulated markets across major asset classes. Explore movers, sentiment-style indicators and sector groupings, then practise with $100,000 virtual cash. Data may be simulated or delayed and is for education only.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

What is on the markets page

The markets page lists every instrument available in the simulator, grouped by asset class: US equities, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds, major and minor forex pairs, and commodities. Each row shows a generated practice price and practice change, and links to a dedicated page for that instrument. Changes are seeded initially and then describe the latest generated update, not a measured daily return.

The Markets page uses simulated practice prices and estimated changes for visual feedback. Provider-backed, delayed or cached data may appear elsewhere on TradeHQ and is labelled separately when available. This is a learning environment, not a market-data terminal — do not use these quotes for any real decision.

How to choose what to practise first
Start with something you already understand as a customer or user — a retailer, an index ETF, or a currency you have actually spent.
Prefer liquid, well-covered instruments. Thin instruments punish beginners with wide spreads and erratic prices.
Choose a manageable set of instruments and record what each exercise tests. No fixed study period establishes competence.
Read the instrument's guide page before the first practice order so you know what typically moves it.
Asset classes explained briefly
Stocks: fractional ownership of a listed company; move on earnings, guidance, sector rotation and rates.
ETFs: funds with stated holdings and objectives. Diversification, concentration, leverage and product structure affect risk.
Crypto: 24/7 markets with no closing bell, high volatility and a strong link to overall market liquidity.
Forex: relative pricing of two currencies; driven by rate differentials, inflation prints and risk appetite.
Commodities: exposures linked to physical goods, supply, demand and seasonal conditions. Company earnings and equity prices can also have seasonal influences.
Reading a market list without being misled

A percentage move needs a clearly stated interval, observation source and comparison sample. A 3% move can have different meanings for different instruments and periods; it is not a permanent volatility category. Generated practice changes do not establish a real-market daily range.

Volume describes trading activity when it is supplied by a valid market-data source. It does not establish the identity or intentions of buyers and sellers, or prove that a price move will continue or reverse. Simulated or unavailable volume cannot confirm an actual market event.

Things that trip beginners on a markets screen
Assuming a large recent gain predicts the next price move; an observed change does not determine future returns or a suitable entry.
Assuming a low nominal price means an asset is 'cheap' — price per unit says nothing about value.
Treating any ETF as automatically low-risk: sector funds and concentrated funds still carry market and holding-specific risks.
Ignoring market hours: equities gap overnight, crypto trades continuously, forex has session-driven liquidity.
References and related pages

Educational simulation only — not financial advice. Virtual money; no brokerage transactions. Quotes may be delayed, cached, unavailable or fixed simulator values; generated charts are labelled separately. Practice results do not predict investment outcomes.

Learning notes: Markets Overview

Browse 170 simulated markets across major asset classes. Explore movers, sentiment-style indicators and sector groupings, then practise with $100,000 virtual cash. Data may be simulated or delayed and is for education only.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

What is on the markets page

The markets page lists every instrument available in the simulator, grouped by asset class: US equities, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds, major and minor forex pairs, and commodities. Each row shows a generated practice price and practice change, and links to a dedicated page for that instrument. Changes are seeded initially and then describe the latest generated update, not a measured daily return.

The Markets page uses simulated practice prices and estimated changes for visual feedback. Provider-backed, delayed or cached data may appear elsewhere on TradeHQ and is labelled separately when available. This is a learning environment, not a market-data terminal — do not use these quotes for any real decision.

How to choose what to practise first
Start with something you already understand as a customer or user — a retailer, an index ETF, or a currency you have actually spent.
Prefer liquid, well-covered instruments. Thin instruments punish beginners with wide spreads and erratic prices.
Choose a manageable set of instruments and record what each exercise tests. No fixed study period establishes competence.
Read the instrument's guide page before the first practice order so you know what typically moves it.
Asset classes explained briefly
Stocks: fractional ownership of a listed company; move on earnings, guidance, sector rotation and rates.
ETFs: funds with stated holdings and objectives. Diversification, concentration, leverage and product structure affect risk.
Crypto: 24/7 markets with no closing bell, high volatility and a strong link to overall market liquidity.
Forex: relative pricing of two currencies; driven by rate differentials, inflation prints and risk appetite.
Commodities: exposures linked to physical goods, supply, demand and seasonal conditions. Company earnings and equity prices can also have seasonal influences.
Reading a market list without being misled

A percentage move needs a clearly stated interval, observation source and comparison sample. A 3% move can have different meanings for different instruments and periods; it is not a permanent volatility category. Generated practice changes do not establish a real-market daily range.

Volume describes trading activity when it is supplied by a valid market-data source. It does not establish the identity or intentions of buyers and sellers, or prove that a price move will continue or reverse. Simulated or unavailable volume cannot confirm an actual market event.

Things that trip beginners on a markets screen
Assuming a large recent gain predicts the next price move; an observed change does not determine future returns or a suitable entry.
Assuming a low nominal price means an asset is 'cheap' — price per unit says nothing about value.
Treating any ETF as automatically low-risk: sector funds and concentrated funds still carry market and holding-specific risks.
Ignoring market hours: equities gap overnight, crypto trades continuously, forex has session-driven liquidity.

Learning notes: Markets Overview

Browse 170 simulated markets across major asset classes. Explore movers, sentiment-style indicators and sector groupings, then practise with $100,000 virtual cash. Data may be simulated or delayed and is for education only.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

What is on the markets page

The markets page lists every instrument available in the simulator, grouped by asset class: US equities, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds, major and minor forex pairs, and commodities. Each row shows a generated practice price and practice change, and links to a dedicated page for that instrument. Changes are seeded initially and then describe the latest generated update, not a measured daily return.

The Markets page uses simulated practice prices and estimated changes for visual feedback. Provider-backed, delayed or cached data may appear elsewhere on TradeHQ and is labelled separately when available. This is a learning environment, not a market-data terminal — do not use these quotes for any real decision.

How to choose what to practise first
Start with something you already understand as a customer or user — a retailer, an index ETF, or a currency you have actually spent.
Prefer liquid, well-covered instruments. Thin instruments punish beginners with wide spreads and erratic prices.
Choose a manageable set of instruments and record what each exercise tests. No fixed study period establishes competence.
Read the instrument's guide page before the first practice order so you know what typically moves it.
Asset classes explained briefly
Stocks: fractional ownership of a listed company; move on earnings, guidance, sector rotation and rates.
ETFs: funds with stated holdings and objectives. Diversification, concentration, leverage and product structure affect risk.
Crypto: 24/7 markets with no closing bell, high volatility and a strong link to overall market liquidity.
Forex: relative pricing of two currencies; driven by rate differentials, inflation prints and risk appetite.
Commodities: exposures linked to physical goods, supply, demand and seasonal conditions. Company earnings and equity prices can also have seasonal influences.
Reading a market list without being misled

A percentage move needs a clearly stated interval, observation source and comparison sample. A 3% move can have different meanings for different instruments and periods; it is not a permanent volatility category. Generated practice changes do not establish a real-market daily range.

Volume describes trading activity when it is supplied by a valid market-data source. It does not establish the identity or intentions of buyers and sellers, or prove that a price move will continue or reverse. Simulated or unavailable volume cannot confirm an actual market event.

Things that trip beginners on a markets screen
Assuming a large recent gain predicts the next price move; an observed change does not determine future returns or a suitable entry.
Assuming a low nominal price means an asset is 'cheap' — price per unit says nothing about value.
Treating any ETF as automatically low-risk: sector funds and concentrated funds still carry market and holding-specific risks.
Ignoring market hours: equities gap overnight, crypto trades continuously, forex has session-driven liquidity.

Learning notes: Markets Overview

Browse 170 simulated markets across major asset classes. Explore movers, sentiment-style indicators and sector groupings, then practise with $100,000 virtual cash. Data may be simulated or delayed and is for education only.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

What is on the markets page

The markets page lists every instrument available in the simulator, grouped by asset class: US equities, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds, major and minor forex pairs, and commodities. Each row shows a generated practice price and practice change, and links to a dedicated page for that instrument. Changes are seeded initially and then describe the latest generated update, not a measured daily return.

The Markets page uses simulated practice prices and estimated changes for visual feedback. Provider-backed, delayed or cached data may appear elsewhere on TradeHQ and is labelled separately when available. This is a learning environment, not a market-data terminal — do not use these quotes for any real decision.

How to choose what to practise first
Start with something you already understand as a customer or user — a retailer, an index ETF, or a currency you have actually spent.
Prefer liquid, well-covered instruments. Thin instruments punish beginners with wide spreads and erratic prices.
Choose a manageable set of instruments and record what each exercise tests. No fixed study period establishes competence.
Read the instrument's guide page before the first practice order so you know what typically moves it.
Asset classes explained briefly
Stocks: fractional ownership of a listed company; move on earnings, guidance, sector rotation and rates.
ETFs: funds with stated holdings and objectives. Diversification, concentration, leverage and product structure affect risk.
Crypto: 24/7 markets with no closing bell, high volatility and a strong link to overall market liquidity.
Forex: relative pricing of two currencies; driven by rate differentials, inflation prints and risk appetite.
Commodities: exposures linked to physical goods, supply, demand and seasonal conditions. Company earnings and equity prices can also have seasonal influences.
Reading a market list without being misled

A percentage move needs a clearly stated interval, observation source and comparison sample. A 3% move can have different meanings for different instruments and periods; it is not a permanent volatility category. Generated practice changes do not establish a real-market daily range.

Volume describes trading activity when it is supplied by a valid market-data source. It does not establish the identity or intentions of buyers and sellers, or prove that a price move will continue or reverse. Simulated or unavailable volume cannot confirm an actual market event.

Things that trip beginners on a markets screen
Assuming a large recent gain predicts the next price move; an observed change does not determine future returns or a suitable entry.
Assuming a low nominal price means an asset is 'cheap' — price per unit says nothing about value.
Treating any ETF as automatically low-risk: sector funds and concentrated funds still carry market and holding-specific risks.
Ignoring market hours: equities gap overnight, crypto trades continuously, forex has session-driven liquidity.

Learning notes: Markets Overview

Browse 170 simulated markets across major asset classes. Explore movers, sentiment-style indicators and sector groupings, then practise with $100,000 virtual cash. Data may be simulated or delayed and is for education only.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

What is on the markets page

The markets page lists every instrument available in the simulator, grouped by asset class: US equities, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds, major and minor forex pairs, and commodities. Each row shows a generated practice price and practice change, and links to a dedicated page for that instrument. Changes are seeded initially and then describe the latest generated update, not a measured daily return.

The Markets page uses simulated practice prices and estimated changes for visual feedback. Provider-backed, delayed or cached data may appear elsewhere on TradeHQ and is labelled separately when available. This is a learning environment, not a market-data terminal — do not use these quotes for any real decision.

How to choose what to practise first
Start with something you already understand as a customer or user — a retailer, an index ETF, or a currency you have actually spent.
Prefer liquid, well-covered instruments. Thin instruments punish beginners with wide spreads and erratic prices.
Choose a manageable set of instruments and record what each exercise tests. No fixed study period establishes competence.
Read the instrument's guide page before the first practice order so you know what typically moves it.
Asset classes explained briefly
Stocks: fractional ownership of a listed company; move on earnings, guidance, sector rotation and rates.
ETFs: funds with stated holdings and objectives. Diversification, concentration, leverage and product structure affect risk.
Crypto: 24/7 markets with no closing bell, high volatility and a strong link to overall market liquidity.
Forex: relative pricing of two currencies; driven by rate differentials, inflation prints and risk appetite.
Commodities: exposures linked to physical goods, supply, demand and seasonal conditions. Company earnings and equity prices can also have seasonal influences.
Reading a market list without being misled

A percentage move needs a clearly stated interval, observation source and comparison sample. A 3% move can have different meanings for different instruments and periods; it is not a permanent volatility category. Generated practice changes do not establish a real-market daily range.

Volume describes trading activity when it is supplied by a valid market-data source. It does not establish the identity or intentions of buyers and sellers, or prove that a price move will continue or reverse. Simulated or unavailable volume cannot confirm an actual market event.

Things that trip beginners on a markets screen
Assuming a large recent gain predicts the next price move; an observed change does not determine future returns or a suitable entry.
Assuming a low nominal price means an asset is 'cheap' — price per unit says nothing about value.
Treating any ETF as automatically low-risk: sector funds and concentrated funds still carry market and holding-specific risks.
Ignoring market hours: equities gap overnight, crypto trades continuously, forex has session-driven liquidity.
